claim_1.claim: CITE-seq analysis of DC-enriched PBMCs from 12 Atlanta cohort subjects (5 healthy controls and 7 COVID-19 patients sampled at day 2, 8, 9, 9, 15, 15, and 16 after symptom onset) showed an early transient interferon-stimulated gene signature including IFI27, IFITM3, and ISG15 in COVID-19, despite absent detectable IFN-α and IFN-β gene expression.

sources.quote: Notably, we detected clusters of T cells and monocytes that were characterized by the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as IFI27, IFITM3, or ISG15 (see C11-C MONO_IFN and C18-T_IFN in fig. S10). These IFN response–enriched clusters emerged only in samples from COVID-19 patients (fig. S12).

Notably, with the exception of modest levels of IFN-γ expression in T and NK cells, we could not detect any expression of IFN-α and -β genes, which is consistent with the functional data demonstrating impaired type I IFN production by pDCs and myeloid cells ( Fig. 2 ). However, there was an enhanced expression of ISGs in patients with COVID-19 ( Fig. 4D ) in spite of an impaired capacity of the innate cells in the blood compartment to produce these cytokines.

Cryopreserved PBMC samples from a total of 12 age-matched subjects in the Atlanta cohort (five healthy controls and seven COVID-19 patients; Table 2 ) were enriched for DCs, stained using a cocktail of 36 DNA-labeled antibodies (table S2), and analyzed using droplet-based single-cell gene expression profiling approaches ( Fig. 4A ).

comparison.finding: COVID-19 samples showed an early transient interferon-stimulated gene signature including IFI27, IFITM3, and ISG15, with IFN response–enriched T-cell and monocyte clusters emerging only in COVID-19 patients, despite absent detectable IFN-α and IFN-β gene expression.

claim_2.claim: Bulk RNA seq analysis of PBMCs from an extended Atlanta cohort of 17 healthy controls and 17 COVID-19 samples showed strong induction of the 33-gene CITE-seq-derived ISG signature in COVID-19 versus healthy donors, while IFN-α and IFN-β transcripts were not detected.

sources.quote: We observed a strong induction of the ISGs in COVID-19 subjects compared with healthy donors in this dataset as well ( Fig. 4G ). Of note, we did not detect expression of genes encoding IFN-α or IFN-β, consistent with the CITE-seq and flow cytometry experiments ( Fig. 4D and Fig. 2 , respectively).

To investigate this further and to independently validate the observations in the CITE-seq analysis, we performed bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of PBMCs in an extended group of subjects (17 COVID-19 patients and 17 healthy controls) from the same cohort.

comparison.finding: strong induction of the 33-gene CITE-seq-derived ISG signature in COVID-19 versus healthy donors; IFN-α and IFN-β transcripts were not detected

claim_3.claim: CyTOF analysis of PBMCs from 52 COVID-19 patients and 62 age- and gender-matched healthy controls across the Hong Kong and Atlanta cohorts showed significantly reduced plasmacytoid dendritic cell frequencies and reduced pS6 in pDCs with decreased IκBα in mDCs in infected individuals versus healthy controls.

sources.quote: There were several differences, but notably the frequency of plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) was significantly reduced in the PBMCs of SARS-CoV-2–infected individuals in both cohorts ( Fig. 1C ).

Additionally, there was reduced expression of pS6 [(phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6), a canonical target of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activation ( 15 )] in pDCs and decreased IκBα—an inhibitor of the signaling of the NF-κB transcription factor—in myeloid dendritic cells (mDCs) ( Fig. 1, D and E ).

We used mass cytometry to assess immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection in 52 COVID-19 patients, who were confirmed positive for viral RNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and 62 age- and gender-matched healthy controls distributed between the two cohorts.

comparison.finding: COVID-19 patients had significantly reduced plasmacytoid dendritic cell frequencies, reduced pS6 in pDCs, and decreased IκBα in mDCs versus healthy controls

claim_4.claim: Flow cytometry of ex vivo stimulated PBMCs from the Atlanta cohort (14 healthy and 17 COVID-19 donors) showed reduced IFN-α and TNF-α production by pDCs and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α responses by mDCs to viral or bacterial TLR ligand cocktails in infected individuals versus healthy controls.

sources.quote: Consistent with our hypothesis, there was reduced production of IFN-α in response to the TLR stimuli in the pDCs of infected individuals compared with those of healthy controls ( Fig. 2A ). The TNF-α response was also significantly reduced in the pDCs of infected individuals, which demonstrates that the pDCs are functionally impaired in COVID-19 infection.

Notably, the response in mDCs as well as that in monocytes were also significantly lower in response to stimulation with a bacterial ligand cocktail (composed of TLR2, TLR4, and TLR5 ligands) or with the viral TLR cocktail ( Fig. 2B and fig. S5).

comparison.finding: infected individuals had reduced IFN-α and TNF-α production by pDCs and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α responses by mDCs to viral or bacterial TLR ligand cocktails versus healthy controls

claim_5.claim: O-link analysis of plasma from the Atlanta cohort showed that 43 cytokines were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 versus healthy controls, with TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and oncostatin M showing strong positive associations with clinical severity and TNFSF14 elevated in COVID-19 but not influenza or RSV.

sources.quote: Of the 92 analytes measured, 71 proteins were detected within the dynamic range of the assay. Of these 71 proteins, 43 cytokines, including IL-6, MCP-3, and CXCL10, were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 infection ( Fig. 3 , top row, and fig. S6).

In addition to IL-6 and other cytokines described previously ( 10 ), we identified three proteins that were significantly enhanced in COVID-19 infection and strongly correlated with clinical severity ( Fig. 3 , bottom row). These were TNFSF14 [LIGHT, a ligand of lymphotoxin B receptor that is highly expressed in human lung fibroblasts and implicated in lung tissue fibrosis and remodeling and inflammation ( 20 )], EN-RAGE [S100A12, a biomarker of pulmonary injury that is implicated in pathogenesis of sepsis-induced ARDS ( 21 )], and oncostatin M [(OSM), a regulator of IL-6]. Of note, the TNFSF14 is distinctively enhanced in the plasma of COVID-19–infected individuals but not in cases of other related pulmonary infections such as influenza (flu) virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) ( Fig. 3 ).
Olink proteomics NA 36 plasma samples (29 patients)

comparison.finding: 43 cytokines were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 versus healthy controls, including IL-6, MCP-3, and CXCL10; TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and oncostatin M were significantly enhanced in COVID-19 infection
TNFSF14 was elevated in COVID-19 but not influenza
TNFSF14 was elevated in COVID-19 but not RSV

claim_6.claim: Flow cytometry of PBMCs analyzed in parallel to the CITE-seq experiment showed reduced HLA-DR protein expression on monocytes and mDCs in COVID-19 patients, most pronounced in subjects with severe disease versus healthy controls.

sources.quote: Consistent with this, we observed a reduction in the expression of the proteins CD86 and human leukocyte antigen class DR (HLA-DR) on monocytes and mDCs of COVID-19 patients, which was most pronounced in subjects with severe COVID-19 infection ( Fig. 5A and fig. S16A).

comparison.finding: HLA-DR protein expression on monocytes and mDCs was reduced in COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls, with the reduction most pronounced in subjects with severe disease

claim_7.claim: Q-PCR analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher bacterial DNA, measured as bacterial 16S rRNA gene product, in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls.

sources.quote: Notably, the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16 S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product, and of LPS, as measured by a TLR4-based reporter assay ( Fig. 6, A and B ).
Each dot represents a sample ( n = 18 and 51 for healthy and infected, respectively).

comparison.finding: severe and ICU COVID-19 patients had significantly higher bacterial DNA, measured as bacterial 16S rRNA gene product, than healthy controls

claim_8.claim: Determination of LPS in plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher LPS levels in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls, and these bacterial products correlated with IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM.

sources.quote: Notably, the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16 S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product, and of LPS, as measured by a TLR4-based reporter assay ( Fig. 6, A and B ).
Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between bacterial DNA or LPS and the plasma levels of the inflammatory mediators IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM ( Fig. 6C and fig. S19).
Each dot represents a sample ( n = 18 and 51 for healthy and infected, respectively).

comparison.finding: LPS levels were significantly higher in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls
LPS correlated with IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM

claim_9.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from COVID-19 patients showed significant increases in TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and oncostatin M in severe and ICU patients versus healthy controls, validating the Olink findings.

sources.quote: Given the pronounced and unappreciated observations of the enhanced plasma concentrations of TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM and their correlation to disease severity, we used an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to independently validate these results. Consistent with the multiplex Olink analysis, we found a significant increase of these inflammatory mediators in the plasma of severe and intensive care unit (ICU) COVID-19 patients.
Furthermore, we found a correlation between multiplex analysis by Olink and the ELISA results (fig. S7).

comparison.finding: TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and oncostatin M were significantly increased in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls, consistent with Olink findings
